Specifications describe what an OSS system is designed to do; the work behind the build is how we make that design ready to deliver. If you are developing a rugged edge computing application, connect with OSS to discuss its requirements and the practical work involved in taking it from design to delivery.
body_markdown:
**By Fabrizio Sardo, Vice President of Operations**


To understand what it takes to manufacture a rugged computing system, it helps to start with something unlikely to appear in a product brochure: a thermal pad.


On a drawing, the pad has a precise location; at the workbench, meeting that requirement involves cutting material, positioning it accurately, and assembling the surrounding components. During OSS assembly and cycle-time reviews, these routine tasks prompted questions about whether a cutting fixture or alignment guide might improve consistency, as well as how connector seating, tool access, and test sequencing could influence the build.


Such details rarely appear in a product specification, yet they help determine whether instructions are clear, work is repeatable, and each person has what they need to do the job correctly.


Our customers are understandably focused on performance, from processing and storage to cooling and operation outside the conventional data center, but delivering that capability requires coordination among Engineering, Operations, Quality, and the people who assemble and test OSS systems.


# The Work Starts Before the Workbench


A production date on the schedule does not always mean an order is ready to build. Beyond material availability, planners must consider remaining work, assembly and test capacity, and repair activity that draws on the same people and equipment; Procurement must also account for supplier processes that affect when a part is ready for assembly.


Consider a circuit board requiring conformal coating. Sending it to a processor is only one step, because the drawing must communicate coating and masking requirements, while Procurement, Engineering, and Quality need a shared understanding of the expected result before the board reaches assembly.


That preparation is easy to overlook, but it helps make the production schedule credible. Rather than asking only whether an order is open or materials have arrived, our planning discussions focus on what must be true before the next operation begins, bringing materials, documentation, and floor capacity into the same conversation.


## Where Engineering Intent Meets Manufacturing Reality


A drawing establishes what must be built, but it cannot capture everything an assembler encounters at the workbench. It may show exactly where a component belongs without revealing how easily someone can reach a fastener, handle a cable, or fully seat a connector, questions the people doing the work are often the first to raise.


I see that feedback as an essential part of disciplined manufacturing, rather than a complaint to dismiss or permission to make unapproved changes. When questions reach the right technical owner and the resolution is reflected in the build information, everyone can work from the same approved understanding.


Manufacturing engineering helps turn those observations into practical improvement opportunities by studying builds, cycle times, and tooling to identify ways to make work more consistent. Our thermal-pad review generated ideas such as a cutting fixture or alignment guide, but an idea must be evaluated before it becomes standard practice; proposing an improvement and demonstrating its value are not the same thing.


The goal is a process people can understand, execute, and repeat without compromising the design.


## What It Takes to Call a System Ready


A system may look complete when assembly ends, but readiness for delivery depends on more than its appearance. Depending on the configuration, setup and acceptance testing still must follow the applicable procedure, making test equipment, technician availability, and engineering support as important to scheduling as assembly capacity.


When a test result needs investigation, Test, Engineering, Production, and Quality may each hold part of the answer. At the same time, the hardware configuration, applicable procedure, and recorded results must remain aligned; without that traceability, we cannot reliably establish what was tested and what was verified.


Even a system that has passed testing may not be ready to ship, because packaging, release documentation, and customer-specific conditions still require attention. There are times when a shipment should be held while a requirement or document is clarified, and those decisions deserve the same care as earlier technical work.


By the time a customer sees the completed system, the questions raised at the bench, the supplier requirements clarified upstream, and the test and release records reviewed are largely invisible. Although different teams make these decisions at different points, their combined judgment shapes what ultimately leaves our facility.


I do not view Operations as the department that takes over once Engineering completes a design; our role is to help turn engineering intent into hardware that can be built consistently, tested appropriately, documented accurately, and delivered to the customer. That work depends on people throughout OSS whose contributions may never appear in a product launch, but whose judgment affects every build.


Specifications describe what an OSS system is designed to do; the work behind the build is how we make that design ready to deliver.


If you are developing a rugged edge computing application, connect with OSS to discuss its requirements and the practical work involved in taking it from design to delivery.
